definition: Extra charge on top of the line-haul rate: detention, layover, lumper, TONU.
A fixed pickup or delivery time slot. The opposite is FCFS.
Shipper’s document listing the freight; receipt and carriage contract, signed at pickup.
Someone who works within a carrier’s organization under a continuing agreement. A carrier-side dispatcher aims to be this.
Licensed middleman who arranges transport between shippers and carriers for compensation.
Company with authority that owns or operates trucks and hauls freight for hire.
A status call or text with the driver: location, loaded, ETA.
Certificate of insurance: proof the carrier’s insurance is active.
The receiver of the freight.
Empty miles driven without paid freight, e.g. to reach a pickup.
Payment for waiting too long at a shipper or receiver, if the RC allows it.
Electronic logging device: records the driver’s hours of service.
Estimated time of arrival. Always give it with a time zone.
Selling invoices to a factoring company for fast cash, minus a fee.
First come, first served: no appointment, but open hours.
Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, the U.S. trucking regulator.
Hours of service: federal limits on driving and duty time.
An origin–destination route, e.g. Chicago → Atlanta.
Online marketplace of posted loads, e.g. DAT, Truckstop.
A third party paid to unload freight at a receiver.
FMCSA operating-authority docket number, still widely used in 2026.
Notice of assignment: tells brokers to pay a carrier’s factoring company.
A driver who owns his truck and often his own authority.
Proof of delivery: the BOL signed by the receiver.
The broker–carrier agreement for one load: rate, stops, terms.
Rate per mile = pay ÷ miles.
The company sending the freight.
Truck order not used: payment when a booked load is cancelled after the truck is dispatched, if the RC allows it.
FMCSA identifier for a company operating commercial vehicles; its safety record is tied to it.
Suspension using air bags for a smoother ride (VA, RA).
Wood or other material built around cargo to stop movement.
Straight truck with an enclosed cargo box.
Federal formula limiting weight on axle groups by their spacing.
Reefer unit runs all the time.
Trailer floor or space is full before reaching the weight limit.
Van with sliding side curtains for side loading (VC).
Reefer unit switches off at setpoint, restarts when needed.
Height of a flatbed or step-deck deck above the ground.
How far a tarp hangs down the side: 4′, 6′, 8′.
Leaving one trailer and taking another instead of waiting to load.
Material used to fill gaps or support cargo (wood, airbags).
Metal rails on van walls for straps and load bars.
Coupling plate on the tractor that holds the trailer’s kingpin.
Freight loaded loose on the floor, not on pallets.
Gross vehicle weight rating: maximum loaded weight of a vehicle.
Pin under the trailer’s nose that locks into the fifth wheel.
Legs that support a dropped trailer.
Powered platform that lowers freight to the ground.
Bar wedged across a van to hold freight in place.
Freight exceeding legal width, height, length or weight.
Hand tool for moving pallets.
Cargo weight a truck can legally carry.
Tractor pulling a trailer it doesn’t own (PO).
Cooling a reefer trailer before loading, when required.
Refrigerated, temperature-controlled trailer or truck.
The temperature the reefer unit is set to hold.
Flatbed with an upper and a lower deck (SD).
Truck with cab and cargo body on one frame.
Pair of axles. Trailer tandems often slide.
Empty weight of a vehicle or trailer.
Strap, chain or similar used to secure cargo.
Reaching the weight limit before the space is full.
Working load limit of a tiedown.
The return direction of a lane, often with fewer or cheaper loads.
Interstate that circles a city (even-first-digit 3-digit number).
Official crossing point with Mexico or Canada.
Official U.S. regions: Northeast, Midwest, South, West.
A route with large, steady freight volumes.
Central, Eastern, Mountain, Pacific time.
Load-board region code Z0–Z9 used for searches.
U.S. summer time, second Sunday in March to first Sunday in November.
Deadhead to origin / from destination on a load board.
The direction where freight is plentiful and pays well.
The time standard the driver’s log must use.
City or area that generates freight all year.
An area where loads outnumber trucks right now.
Interstate highway number.
Freight still under customs control; specialist handling.
Origin → destination pair, e.g. Dallas → Atlanta.
Mountain Standard Time; Arizona uses it all year.
Primary Highway Freight System (FHWA).
Pakistan Standard Time, UTC+5, no DST.
Actual driving miles, always more than straight-line distance.
A state with two time zones.
Short interstate branching off a main route (odd first digit).
Dallas–Houston–San Antonio/Austin freight region.
Road legal and safe for large trucks.
Maximum driving after 10 consecutive hours off.
Period after coming on duty; no driving after its end.
Required after 8 cumulative hours of driving.
34+ consecutive hours off duty that resets the 60/70 cycle.
On-duty limit over 7 or 8 consecutive days.
Unexpected conditions allowing up to 2 extra hours.
Forcing a driver to break safety rules; banned by 49 CFR 390.6.
On-duty hours left in the 7/8-day period.
Empty miles to reach a pickup; uses the same clocks.
ELD figure: driving hours remaining today.
Electronic logging device recording duty status.
First come, first served: a window instead of a fixed time.
Hours of service: federal driver work-time rules.
Time standard used on the driver’s log.
Driver waits while freight is loaded or unloaded.
Not working.
Working but not driving: loading, inspections, waiting.
Off-duty personal use of the truck; never to advance a load.
Record of duty status (the log).
150 air miles / 14 h: time records instead of logs.
Time remaining in the 14-hour window.
Rest in the truck’s sleeping compartment.
7+ h sleeper + 2+ h rest = the 10-hour rest.
Two drivers taking turns so the truck keeps moving.
On-duty movement inside a yard.
Standard certificate-of-insurance form.
FMCSA permission to operate for hire (common/contract/broker).
Bodily injury and property damage (auto liability) insurance.
Insurer’s liability filing with FMCSA.
Filing naming process agents in each state.
Covers the freight being hauled.
Party (e.g. a broker) named on a COI.
Certificate of insurance.
Contract between the carrier and its dispatcher.
MC / MX / FF authority number.
Employer Identification Number (tax ID).
Selling invoices to a factor for fast cash.
FMCSA Licensing & Insurance records.
Federal identity-verification service used by Motus.
Carrier census form; update every 2 years.
FMCSA’s registration system (2025–26).
Notice of assignment: pay the factor.
Insurance for trailers the carrier pulls but doesn’t own.
Order barring a company, driver or vehicle from operating.
FMCSA public company snapshot lookup.
Policy covers only listed vehicles.
FMCSA Safety Measurement System.
FMCSA company identifier.
Letter after a new USDOT number showing entity type.
IRS form giving a taxpayer ID to a payer.
Time since a posting was created or refreshed.
Notification when new matching loads appear.
Load that brings the truck back toward home or a good market.
Book online without a call; still produces a rate confirmation.
DAT broker credit rating.
Deadhead to origin / from destination.
Average payment time.
Load whose invoice a factor will buy.
Full or partial load.
Online marketplace of loads and trucks.
Advertise available capacity.
Loads visible only to selected carriers.
Rate ÷ miles (loaded, or total including deadhead).
The broker’s load number on the board.
Stored search criteria for quick refresh.
Only show loads posted in the last X hours.
Loaded miles from pickup to delivery.
DAT tool suggesting triangular routes.
Region code (Z0–Z9) for searches.
One total that includes fuel.
Rate per total mile where revenue after fees equals cost.
Rate agreed for months between shipper and carrier.
All costs ÷ all miles in a period.
Money taken off the pay for a broken rule.
Dispatcher’s pay, often a % of gross.
U.S. Energy Information Administration; publishes weekly diesel prices.
Selling invoices for fast pay, for a fee (recourse / non-recourse).
Paid every week regardless of miles.
Pay that follows the diesel price.
Strong direction / weaker return direction.
Base rate without fuel.
Load posts ÷ truck posts, per market and equipment.
DAT’s hot/cold supply-demand map.
Fixed + variable cost per mile.
Trip revenue ÷ days the truck is committed.
All-in rate ÷ (deadhead + loaded).
DAT’s tool for recent paid lane rates.
One-off price for a single load.
Break-even plus the carrier’s profit cushion.
Grows with each mile.
Lowest rate you’d accept: usually break-even.
Broker’s $75,000 surety bond filing.
Broker’s $75,000 trust fund filing.
Notice cancelling a bond or trust.
First number that sets the negotiation range.
Shipment where the parties’ identities are hidden; can be legitimate, but a red flag if you’re asked to misrepresent yourself.
Carrier’s claim against a broker’s surety or trust for unpaid freight.
Re-selling a load taken as a carrier, without authority or disclosure.
Theft where a fake carrier collects real freight.
Free tool for carriers to verify brokers.
Using another company’s MC/DOT or name.
Posing as a real broker with lookalike contacts.
FMCSA Licensing & Insurance: authority and filings.
FMCSA’s National Consumer Complaint Database.
Fake links or messages that steal logins.
FMCSA company snapshot: entity type, status, contacts.
The rate you aim for: target × total miles.
Lowest acceptable rate; usually break-even.
Arranging carriage without broker registration and security; unlawful.
Bill of lading: receipt and contract for the shipment.
Status update from the driver or to the broker.
Signed delivery with no shortage or damage noted.
The driver’s load instructions.
Swap trailers instead of waiting to load.
Shortage, overage, damage or refusal noted on the POD.
First come, first served: no fixed appointment.
Invoice + rate con + POD + receipts.
Driver waits while freight is loaded or unloaded.
Over, short and damaged.
Proof of delivery: the signed BOL or delivery receipt.
Pickup or delivery reference numbers.
Broker pays early for a fee.
Rate confirmation: the load contract.
Numbered tag locking the trailer doors.
Shipper load and count.

Location sharing with the broker (ELD or app).
Extra charge beyond the linehaul.
HOS exception adding up to 2 h when unexpected conditions arise.
49 U.S.C. 14706: carrier liability for cargo loss or damage.
Written demand with shipment, liability and amount.
Paid waiting after free time.
Driver helps load or unload, if agreed and paid.
Waiting allowed before detention starts (often 2 h).
Truck held overnight or to the next day.
Paid unloading crew at a facility.
Payment code issued so a driver can pay a fee.
Message telling the broker free time is ending.
Broker holding payment against a claim.
Vehicle or driver barred from moving until fixed.
Moving freight after a breakdown, arranged by the broker.
Selling damaged freight to reduce a loss.
Truck ordered, not used.
